text: Chapter 1 modeled individual configuration items — a server, an application, a database — each a real row under cmdb_ci. Those rows describe what exists, but on their own they say nothing about how those things connect to each other. This lesson covers the table that captures that connection: cmdb_rel_ci.

Every row on cmdb_rel_ci is one relationship between exactly two CIs — a parent, a child, and a relationship type. If an application genuinely runs on a server, that fact only exists on the platform if someone, or Discovery later in this course, actually created that record. An admin who never touches this table has a CMDB that's accurate about assets and blind to how they fit together.

The type isn't a single word like 'depends on.' It's a directional pair, stored on the cmdb_rel_type table, describing the same relationship from each side. 'Runs on, Runs' read from the parent says it runs on the child; read from the child, it says the child runs the parent — same relationship, two correct readings, depending which CI you start from.

ServiceNow ships a standard set of these pairs so admins and Discovery aren't inventing new ones constantly: Depends on and Used by for the general case, Runs on and Runs for application-to-server, Hosted on and Hosts for a VM on its hypervisor host or a CI on cloud infrastructure. Reusing the standard set keeps the data consistent enough for reports and scripts to rely on.

Direction is not cosmetic. A database doesn't run on an application — the application depends on the database. Get that backward in the CMDB, and a later query asking what breaks if the database goes down will miss the application entirely, or point the dependency arrow the wrong way.

That's the real mechanism this whole chapter, and this course's later impact-analysis work, sits on top of. Next: the Dependency View, where this relationship graph actually becomes visible on screen, and how Service Mapping can build that graph automatically instead of requiring every relationship to be documented by hand.
